concepts.title: Caste in the Past: Varna, Jati and the Defining Features

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Caste in the Past: Varna, Jati and the Defining Features' refers to.
questions.a: Caste is an institution tied to the Indian subcontinent, known in Indian languages through two words: varna, a four-fold all-India division into brahmana, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra (with the excluded panchamas), and jati, the regional sub-classification of hundreds of castes and sub-castes. Its defining features are that caste is fixed by birth, marriage is endogamous within the group, food and food-sharing rules apply, castes sit in a hierarchy of rank, sub-castes create segmental organisation, and occupations were hereditary.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Caste in the Past: Varna, Jati and the Defining Features'.
questions.a: The early Vedic varna order of roughly 900-500 BC was loose and open to movement; only in the post-Vedic period did birth-fixed rigid caste appear.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Caste in the Past: Varna, Jati and the Defining Features', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: caste_terms = varna (four_fold_all_india) + jati (regional_subcastes) ; features = birth + endogamy + food_rules + hierarchy + segmental + hereditary_occupation

concepts.title: Principles of the Caste System: Separation, Hierarchy, Purity and Pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Principles of the Caste System: Separation, Hierarchy, Purity and Pollution' refers to.
questions.a: The caste system combines two sets of principles: difference and separation, which keep every caste strictly apart through rules on marriage, food sharing, interaction and occupation, and wholism with hierarchy, under which castes exist only within the societal whole and occupy an ordered rung on a ladder from highest to lowest. This ranking rests on the opposition of purity and pollution - castes nearer the sacred rank high, the ritually polluting rank low - while material power usually tracks social status, and defeated groups were often pushed to low caste status.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Principles of the Caste System: Separation, Hierarchy, Purity and Pollution'.
questions.a: Castes are complementary and non-competing - each has a fixed place no other caste may take - so the system works as a social division of labour without mobility.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Principles of the Caste System: Separation, Hierarchy, Purity and Pollution', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: caste_logic = separation_and_difference + wholism_and_hierarchy ; rank_basis = purity_vs_pollution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Colonialism and Caste' refers to.
questions.a: Colonial rule reshaped caste deeply: British administrators ran methodical surveys of customs, counted castes in the census begun in the 1860s and made ten-yearly from 1881, and the 1901 Census under Herbert Risley recorded the social rank order of castes, provoking hundreds of petitions claiming higher positions. The Government of India Act of 1935 gave legal recognition to scheduled lists of castes and tribes for special state treatment, which is how the labels Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes were born - leading many scholars to call today's caste more a product of colonialism than of ancient tradition.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Colonialism and Caste'.
questions.a: Once caste identities began to be counted and officially recorded, institutions that had been fluid became rigid - counting changed the thing counted.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Colonialism and Caste', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: colonial_contributions = caste_surveys + census_rank_order (Risley 1901) + scheduled_lists (1935 Act)

questions.q: How many ten-yearly census exercises ran from the 1881 census up to the Census Report 2011? Use the method 'Counting the Colonial Census Cycles'. Work with: census_first_year = 1000, census_interval = 360, census_last_year = 1000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of census_cycles.
questions.a: 0 units

questions.q: Compute the number of census cycles between 1881 and 2011 given the ten-year interval. Use the method 'Counting the Colonial Census Cycles'. Work with: census_first_year = 50, census_interval = 20, census_last_year = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of census_cycles.
questions.a: 0 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Counting the Colonial Census Cycles' refers to.
questions.a: The colonial census of caste became a regular ten-yearly exercise from 1881 onwards, and independent India continued the practice; the number of census cycles between two census years follows directly from the span of years divided by the ten-year interval.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Counting the Colonial Census Cycles'.
questions.a: Divide the years between the first and last census by the interval to get the count of ten-yearly exercises.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Counting the Colonial Census Cycles', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: census_cycles = census_span / census_interval

concepts.title: Caste in the Present: Politics, Sanskritisation and the Dominant Caste

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Caste in the Present: Politics, Sanskritisation and the Dominant Caste' refers to.
questions.a: Independent India abolished caste in law yet caste stayed central: democratic politics absorbed caste calculus and caste-based parties rose from the 1980s; M.N. Srinivas's concepts name the processes - sanskritisation, where a middle or lower caste raises status by copying the ritual and social practices of a higher caste, and dominant caste, the numerous intermediate castes such as Yadavs, Vokkaligas, Reddys, Marathas, Jats and Patidars who gained landrights through post-Independence land reforms and turned numbers into political power. Caste also turned paradoxical - invisible for privileged upper castes who credit merit, all too visible for scheduled and backward castes whose identity anchors reservations and who still face discrimination; endogamy survived modernisation best of all.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Caste in the Present: Politics, Sanskritisation and the Dominant Caste'.
questions.a: Recruitment in mills, urban neighbourhoods and politics kept organising along caste and kinship lines, while marriage within caste remained largely untouched by change.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Caste in the Present: Politics, Sanskritisation and the Dominant Caste', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: new_concepts = sanskritisation + dominant_caste ; visibility = invisible_for_upper_caste_elite + visible_for_scheduled_backward_castes

concepts.title: Tribal Communities: Classification by Permanent and Acquired Traits

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Tribal Communities: Classification by Permanent and Acquired Traits' refers to.
questions.a: Tribe is a modern label for some of the oldest inhabitants of the subcontinent, first defined negatively - no written-scripture religion, no state, no sharp class divisions. Positive classification uses permanent traits (region, language, physical characteristics, ecological habitat) and acquired traits (mode of livelihood and degree of assimilation into Hindu society). By language tribes fall into Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austric and Tibeto-Burman groups; by race into Negrito, Australoid, Mongoloid, Dravidian and Aryan categories.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Tribal Communities: Classification by Permanent and Acquired Traits'.
questions.a: Tribes range from about seven million members to Andamanese islanders under a hundred, with Gonds, Bhils, Santhals, Oraons, Minas, Bodos and Mundas each a million strong.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Tribal Communities: Classification by Permanent and Acquired Traits', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: permanent_traits = region + language + physical_characteristics + ecological_habitat ; acquired_traits = livelihood + assimilation_into_hindu_society

concepts.title: Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth

questions.q: Compute the tribal population of India in 2001 if the national population was 1028 million and the tribal share 8.2 per cent. Use the method 'Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth'. Work with: national_population = 5000, tribal_share = 0.4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of tribal_count.
questions.a: 20 units

questions.q: How many million tribal persons did the 2011 Census report for the country? Use the method 'Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth'. Work with: national_population = 12000, tribal_share = 0.45. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of tribal_count.
questions.a: 54 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth' refers to.
questions.a: Census figures fix the tribal presence in numbers: about 8.2 per cent of India's population, roughly 84 million persons at the 2001 Census, rose to 8.6 per cent, about 104 million persons, in the Census Report 2011; about 85 per cent of tribals live in middle India and over 11 per cent of the remainder in the North-East, where states other than Assam exceed 30 per cent tribal share and some cross 60 per cent.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth'.
questions.a: Multiply India's population by the tribal percentage to recover the census count of about 84 million in 2001 and 104 million in 2011.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Tribal Population Shares and Census Growth', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: tribal_count = national_population * tribal_share / 100

concepts.title: Tribal Identity, Development Costs and the Caste-Tribe Debate

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Tribal Identity, Development Costs and the Caste-Tribe Debate' refers to.
questions.a: Scholars first debated whether tribes sit at one end of a continuum with caste-peasant society or differ wholly because they lack purity-pollution ideas, but by the 1970s every standard criterion - size, isolation, religion, livelihood - had failed to hold the distinction, and some now see tribes as secondary products of colonial contact rather than pristine societies. National development, with its large dams, factories and mines sited in mineral-rich forest areas, made tribals pay a disproportionate price through dispossession, deforestation, private property in land and heavy in-migration - Tripura's tribal share halved in a decade - while tribal identities today centre on resistance, statehood wins like Jharkhand and Chattisgarh, and a rising educated middle class asserting culture and resource control.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Tribal Identity, Development Costs and the Caste-Tribe Debate'.
questions.a: Tribal identities come from interaction with the mainstream, not from primordial traits, and the two great movement issues are control over land and forests and ethnic-cultural identity.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Tribal Identity, Development Costs and the Caste-Tribe Debate', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: development_costs = land_dispossession + forest_loss + in_migration ; identity_bases = resistance + statehood + educated_middle_class

concepts.title: Family and Kinship: Nuclear, Extended and Diverse Forms

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Family and Kinship: Nuclear, Extended and Diverse Forms' refers to.
questions.a: The family is at once a space of warmth and care and a site of conflict and violence; structurally it may be nuclear - one set of parents and their children - or extended, the so-called joint family with more than one couple and often more than two generations, though the joint family was never the dominant Indian form and the very term is a translated, not native, category. Residence rules divide matrilocal from patrilocal societies, inheritance rules divide matrilineal from patrilineal descent, and patriarchal authority contrasts with matriarchy, which remains theoretical since no historical or anthropological evidence finds societies where women dominate - only matrilineal ones where women inherit but do not control property.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Family and Kinship: Nuclear, Extended and Diverse Forms'.
questions.a: Family structure moves with social change - male migration makes women-headed Himalayan villages, and software-industry schedules bring grandparents in as care-givers.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Family and Kinship: Nuclear, Extended and Diverse Forms', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: family_structures = nuclear + extended_joint ; rules = matrilocal_vs_patrilocal + matrilineal_vs_patrilineal + patriarchy_vs_matriarchy
